cases.blocker_or_note: Ledger: 'collect the cabin class of each proposed segment and test that the set has exactly one member.' Textbook all-elements-equal-at-sub-path over the proposed segment array at /cabinClass; literal-free, no outer reference. Vacuous truth on a 0- or 1-segment itinerary is the right answer here.

Cardinality of the passenger array, consumed by 'in [1,2,3,4,5]' (at least one, at most five). A boolean exists/every quantifier cannot produce or bound a cardinality; you would need a count operator with a literal bound (or ordinal indexing, e.g. 'no element at index 5', which is outside element-rooted exists/every).

'Build the per-passenger itinerary ... and test all itineraries for equality' — set-of-values-has-one-member over passengers at a composite sub-path. Reachable by a uniform operator only if the caller materializes passengers[]/itinerary as a sub-object and canonicalizes segment order, since §7 equality on arrays is order-sensitive; the projection itself is data preparation, not a quantifier.

Classify-then-count: per-element type resolved by profile lookup, then cardinality of matches against 'at most one' (in [0,1]). The classification could be denormalized onto each element as a literal-comparable field, but the counting cannot — exists/every yields a boolean, not a number, and cannot express 'at most one matching element'.
Same classify-then-count construct against 'at most one credit card' (in [0,1]). Blocker is the cardinality of matching elements, not the per-element predicate.
Same classify-then-count against 'at most three gift cards' (in [0,1,2,3]). Cardinality of matching elements is the missing device.

Every proposed payment-method id must be a member of the profile's stored payment-method list — a join. An element-rooted inner predicate cannot see the profile collection, and §7 'in' requires a literal non-empty array as the condition value, so a runtime-supplied list cannot serve as the right operand.

Ordinal/interpretive selection of ONE element from EACH of two segment lists (stored and proposed), then comparison of the two selected airport values. Three blockers: selection of a distinguished element (not every/exists), access to two collections at once, and a pointer-to-pointer comparison with no literal. Overlaid with a policy reading of 'origin' (outbound-leg start vs first-segment origin).

Same two-list distinguished-element selection and pointer-to-pointer comparison as preservesOrigin, with a heavier interpretive step: for a round trip 'destination' must be read as the turnaround point (arrival of the outbound leg), not the final arrival.

Must derive a classification VALUE (one way / round trip) from the proposed segment list — a first-vs-last cross-element comparison over the whole list — and then compare that derived value against another fact (the stored trip type). Quantifiers emit booleans, not classifications, and §7 has no fact-to-fact comparison.

Set EQUALITY between the segments the user named and the reservation's full segment list — bidirectional membership (every reservation segment named, and vice versa), i.e. a join in both directions. The inner predicate would have to reference the other collection. Ledger also flags the degenerate one-segment case, where a naive 'which segments did they name?' reading is unsound.

Cardinality of TWO collections compared to each other (requested roster vs current roster), not to a literal bound — so not even a bounded count operator suffices. Compounded by step 1 (constructing the post-change roster from natural language) and step 4 (deciding whether substitution or add-then-remove counts as a count change), which is policy application.

Pure disjunction over segments of a per-segment boolean field: exists(segment) where segment/cancelledByAirline equals true. Element-rooted, literal right operand, no outer scope. The only clean exists case in the census.

Cardinality of the stored passengers array. Note the pack only tests not-equals null (availability); the VALUE is consumed as an arithmetic operand ($100/$50 x N) carried in the outcome text and the io.onword.compensation extension. So this needs a cardinality operator that emits a number, which is strictly beyond any boolean quantifier — no bound is even applied.

Two-stage reach: (a) ordinal/temporal selection of the initial charge out of the order's multi-entry payment history (not later refunds or adjustments), then (b) resolving that id against the profile's payment-method list to obtain a type — a join. Emits a value (compared to 'gift_card' by the pack), not a boolean, so no quantifier shape applies. 'The original payment method' is also undefined by the policy.

Consumed as equals 1 / not-equals 1 — an exactly-one test on the cardinality of the methods the user named. Exists/every cannot distinguish one from two; expressing exactly-N requires counting (or pairwise distinctness plus a bound).

Select the original charge out of the order's payment history (ordinal selection, undefined term 'original'), then an identity test between two fact pointers. Both /order/originalPaymentMethodId and /request/newPaymentMethodId are present in the facts document yet unreadable by any condition, because §7 fact conditions compare a pointer only against a literal.

Element-by-element (aligned) comparison of the old-item list against the new-item list: two catalog lookups per pair to resolve product ids, then equality per pair, then conjunction. Even with the pairs pre-zipped (as facts.example.json does, with originalProductId/newProductId on each substitution element), the inner predicate is a field-vs-field comparison — §7 admits no pointer-to-pointer operand, only literals. Also commits to reading 'same product' as same product id.

Per-pair inequality of two option maps (originalOptions vs newOptions), conjoined over the list. Field-vs-field comparison within the element, so not literal-comparable; additionally the policy does not fix whether 'different product option' means any differing value or a wholly different option set, so the reading is fixed outside the pack.

every(substitution) where newItemAvailable equals true. The catalog availability lookup is per-element data preparation that denormalizes onto the element (facts.example.json already carries newItemAvailable per substitution), leaving a literal-valued, element-rooted predicate. The conjunction across the list is exactly what an every operator supplies.

Identify the original charge within the order's payment history (ordinal selection out of a collection), then an identity test against the method the user named. Mechanical but doubly inexpressible: no collection reach and no pointer-to-pointer equality — both /order/originalPaymentMethodId and /refund/providedPaymentMethodId sit in the facts document unread.

Degenerate join: some element of the profile's payment-method list must equal the single named refund destination AND be of type gift card. The exists predicate must compare the element's id against an outer fact (/refund/providedPaymentMethodId), not a literal — outer-scope access is the blocker. Plus the undefined policy term 'existing', which the pack reads as already on this authenticated user's profile.

Resolve each old and each new item id to its parent product id, compare pairwise, AND over the exchange list. Same blocker as R3 allNewItemsSameProduct: the inner predicate is a comparison of two resolved fields, with no literal operand. Interpretive overlay: 'product type' read as catalogue product id.

every(requested new item) where availability equals available. Pure lookup plus aggregation per the ledger, no policy interpretation; once the catalog availability flag is attached to each element (as R3's sibling facts document does), the predicate is element-rooted against a literal and the conjunction is the whole of what is missing.

Per-pair option-map inequality AND-ed over the exchange list — field-vs-field comparison, no literal operand. Also commits to reading 'of different product option' as a hard requirement rather than description.
